People who are in business for themselves will generally have to pay their tax through estimated tax [4.1]. 

You must make estimated tax payments if you meet the requirements to do so (such as owing $1,000 or more after subtracting withholding and refundable credits, and not meeting exceptions based on percentages of prior or current year tax) [4.25]. 

The tax year is divided into four payment periods with the following general due dates:
- **Jan. 1–March 31 period:** Due April 15 [4.26].
- **April 1–May 31 period:** Due June 15 [4.26].
- **June 1–August 31 period:** Due Sept. 15 [4.26].
- **Sept. 1–Dec. 31 period:** Due Jan. 15 of the next year [4.26].

If you do not have income subject to estimated tax until a later payment period, your first payment must be made by the due date for that specific period [4.28]. If a due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, the payment is on time if made on the next day that isn't a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday [4.27]. Additionally, you do not need to make the January 15 payment if you file your Form 1040 or 1040-SR by February 1 and pay the rest of the tax you owe [4.27].

You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code, which generally means keeping records that support items shown on your return until the period of limitations for that return runs out [1.49]. 

The periods of limitations are as follows:
- If you file a return and situations (2), (3), and (4) do not apply, the period is 3 years [1.49].
- If you don’t report income that you should and it is more than 25% of the gross income shown on your return, the period is 6 years [1.49].
- If you file a fraudulent return, there is no limit [1.49].
- If you don’t file a return, there is no limit [1.49].
- If you file a claim for credit or refund after you filed your return, the period is the later of 3 years or 2 years after the tax was paid [1.49].
- If you file a claim for a loss from worthless securities or bad debt deduction, the period is 7 years [1.49].

For property, you must keep records relating to the property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition [1.49]. If you received property in a nontaxable exchange, you must keep the records on both the old and new property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the new property in a taxable disposition [1.49]. Additionally, if you receive a Form W-2, you should keep Copy C until you begin receiving social security benefits [1.47].

If the refund isn’t made within this 45-day period, interest will be paid from the due date of the return or from the date you filed, whichever is later [1.51]. (If you receive a refund because of an amended return, interest is paid from the due date of your original return or the date you filed your original return, whichever is later, to the date you filed the amended return, or up to the payment date if the refund isn't made within 45 days after you file the amended return) [1.54].

Generally, you must file your claim for a credit or refund (amended return) within 3 years after the date you filed your original return or within 2 years after the date you paid the tax, whichever is later [1.54]. Returns filed before the due date (without regard to extensions) are considered filed on the due date [1.54]. These time periods are suspended while you are financially disabled [1.54].

You are eligible to file your 2025 return as a qualifying surviving spouse if you meet all of the following tests:
- You were entitled to file a joint return with your spouse for the year your spouse died (it doesn't matter whether you actually filed a joint return) [2.14].
- Your spouse died in 2023 or 2024 and you didn't remarry before the end of 2025 [2.14].
- You have a child or stepchild (not a foster child) whom you can claim as a dependent or could claim as a dependent except that, for 2025, the child had gross income of $5,200 or more, filed a joint return, or could be claimed as a dependent on someone else's return [2.14].
- This child lived in your home all year, except for temporary absences, with certain exceptions for birth, death, adoption, or kidnapping [2.14].
- You paid more than half of the cost of keeping up a home for the year [2.14].

To figure whether you paid more than half of the cost of keeping up a home, you can determine it by using Worksheet 2-1 (Cost of Keeping Up a Home) [2.12]:
- **Costs you include:** Rent, mortgage interest, real estate taxes, insurance on the home, repairs, utilities, and food eaten in the home [2.12].
- **Costs you don’t include:** Clothing, education, medical treatment, vacations, life insurance, transportation, or the value of your services or those of a member of your household [2.12].

If the total amount you paid is more than the amount others paid, you meet the requirement of paying more than half of the cost of keeping up the home [2.12].

If you had to repay an amount that you included in your income in an earlier year, you may be able to deduct the amount repaid from your income for the year in which you repaid it, or—if the amount repaid is more than $3,000—you may be able to take a credit against your tax for the year in which you repaid it [8.15]. 

Generally, you can claim a deduction or credit only if the repayment qualifies as an expense or loss incurred in your trade or business or in a for-profit transaction [8.15]. The type of deduction you are allowed depends on the type of income you included in the earlier year (such as a business expense on Schedule C or F, a capital loss on Schedule D, or as an other itemized deduction if it was wages, unemployment compensation, or other nonbusiness income over $3,000) [8.15]. Beginning in 2018, miscellaneous itemized deductions can no longer be claimed, so if the amount repaid was $3,000 or less and was previously reported as nonbusiness income, you are not able to deduct it [8.15]. If the amount repaid was more than $3,000 and included under a claim of right, you can choose between taking an other itemized deduction on Schedule A (Form 1040), line 16, or taking a credit, by figuring your tax under both methods and using the one that results in less tax [8.15].

To claim exemption from withholding for 2026, both of the following situations must apply:
- For 2025, you had a right to a refund of all federal income tax withheld because you had no tax liability [4.12].
- For 2026, you expect a refund of all federal income tax withheld because you expect to have no tax liability [4.12].

To claim exemption, you must give your employer a Form W-4 by writing "Exempt" on the form in the space below Step 4(c) and completing the applicable steps of the form [4.12]. 

An exemption is good for only 1 year [4.12]. You must generally give your employer a new Form W-4 by February 15 each year to continue your exemption [4.12].

For a decedent's final tax return, the standard deduction is the same as it would have been had the decedent continued to live [10.2]. However, if the decedent wasn't 65 or older at the time of death, the higher standard deduction for age can't be claimed [10.2]. 

For a single taxpayer who is not 65 or older and not blind (born after January 1, 1961), and assuming no one else can claim them as a dependent, the standard deduction is $15,750 [10.10 (Table 10-1)].

To meet the gross income test for a qualifying relative, the person's gross income for the year must be less than $5,200 [3.17]. 

Gross income is defined as all income in the form of money, property, and services that isn't exempt from tax [3.17]. Specifically:
- For a manufacturing, merchandising, or mining business, gross income is total net sales minus the cost of goods sold, plus any miscellaneous business income [3.17].
- Gross receipts from rental property are gross income, without deducting taxes, repairs, or other expenses [3.17].
- Gross income includes a partner's share of the gross (not net) partnership income [3.17].
- Gross income also includes all taxable unemployment compensation, taxable social security benefits, and certain amounts received as scholarship and fellowship grants (excluding those received by degree candidates and used for required tuition, fees, supplies, books, and equipment) [3.17].

Estimated tax is the method used to pay tax on income that isn’t subject to withholding, which includes income from self-employment [4.23]. 

You don’t have to pay estimated tax for 2026 if you meet all three of the following conditions:
- You had no tax liability for 2025 (your total tax was zero or you didn’t have to file an income tax return).
- You were a U.S. citizen or resident alien for the whole year.
- Your 2025 tax year covered a 12-month period [4.24].

You also don’t have to pay estimated tax if you will pay enough through withholding to keep the amount you owe with your return under $1,000 [4.30].

You don’t have to make estimated tax payments until you have income on which you will owe income tax [4.28]. Depending on when you first have income on which you must pay estimated tax, the general due dates for installment payments are:
- **Before April 1:** Make installments by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15 of the next year [4.28].
- **April 1–May 31:** Make installments by June 15, September 15, and January 15 of the next year [4.28].
- **June 1–August 31:** Make installments by September 15 and January 15 of the next year [4.28].
- **After August 31:** Make the payment by January 15 of the next year [4.28].
